chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: Sir Charles Thompson and the dispute over Robbins' Nest
summary: Thompson left after getting no credit or royalties on the hit tune, which opened the job for Malachi.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I got there and I found out Sir Charles had quit because of a misunderstanding that he had with Illinois over a tune that he had written called "Robbins Nest." It seems as if Illinois had recorded the tune, and I don't know who named it after Fred Robbins, the disk jockey there... So they called it "Robbins Nest." They had some sort of misunderstanding about it, where it seems like it wound up with Sir Charles not

having one cent in his own composition. And from what he told me, he never received any royalties or anything. And the record was a big record. It was one of Illinois Jacquet's biggest records. Now, just what happened as far as the business is concerned, I only know from what Sir Charles told me. But after that, he just sort of seemed not to care too much about playing music any more, or anything else.

But anyway, sometimes, like I said, somebody's misfortune is your good fortune.. And I needed a job, and the fact was, I talked to him about it, and it wasn't a thing that he was regretful about it, because he wasn't going back with Illinois. So I had no guilt about taking anybody's job. Anyway, I was with the band, and I stayed with the band from January to September.
